title: Fishers, a Leper, a Paralytic, and a Tax Collector
summary: After a miraculous catch of fish, Simon Peter falls at Jesus' knees confessing he is a sinful man, and he, James, and John leave everything to follow. Jesus touches and cleanses a man covered with leprosy, forgives and heals a paralyzed man lowered through a roof, and calls the tax collector Levi, whose banquet provokes a dispute with the Pharisees about eating with sinners and about fasting. Jesus answers with images of a doctor, a bridegroom, new garments, and new wine.
story:
Chapter 4 announced Jesus' mission and showed his authority over demons and disease in Capernaum. Now he begins to gather people around him, and the kinds of people he gathers are the point: fishermen who discover they are sinful, a man whose disease has shut him out of community, a paralytic carried by friends, and a despised tax collector with a houseful of friends like him. Luke places the call of Simon after Jesus has already taught in the synagogue, healed Simon's mother-in-law, and become known in the region, so that Simon's decision to leave his nets has a history behind it.

The chapter also introduces the Pharisees and teachers of the law, who will watch and question Jesus through the rest of the Gospel. From 5:17 to 6:11 Luke follows Mark 2:1-3:6 in a series of five controversy stories: forgiveness, table company, fasting, grain picked on the Sabbath, and healing on the Sabbath. The conflict begins not over politics but over forgiveness and fellowship: who has the right to forgive sins, whom God's messenger may eat with, and whether the joy of his presence can be contained in old forms. By the end of chapter 6 his opponents are discussing what to do with him, and the quiet reference to a bridegroom who will be taken away (5:35) is the first shadow of the cross in Luke's account of the ministry.
historical:
The Lake of Gennesaret is Luke's name for the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about 21 kilometers (13 miles) long and 12 wide, fed and drained by the Jordan and lying some 210 meters below sea level. Luke alone calls it a limnē, ‘lake’; Mark and Matthew follow the Hebrew yam and call it a sea. Gennesaret is the fertile plain on the northwest shore, which Josephus praises for its year-round harvests and after which he names the lake (Jewish War 3.506, 3.516-521). The Old Testament calls it the Sea of Kinnereth (Numbers 34:11). Fishing was the lake's industry. Towns such as Bethsaida (‘house of fishing’) and Magdala, which many identify with the Tarichaeae (‘salted fish’) of Josephus, processed and exported fish. K. C. Hanson (Biblical Theology Bulletin 27, 1997) argued that fishing rights were leased and taxed under Herod Antipas, so that fishing families worked in partnerships under a web of brokers and toll collectors; other scholars have questioned how much of that system can be demonstrated for Galilee. Luke's word for Simon's colleagues, partners (metochoi and koinōnoi), fits a family business of more than one boat.

In 1986, during a drought, two fishermen of Kibbutz Ginosar, the brothers Moshe and Yuval Lufan, found the remains of a wooden boat in the mud of the northwest shore. The Galilee Boat is about 8.2 meters (27 feet) long and 2.3 meters wide, dated by radiocarbon to about 40 BC plus or minus 80 years and by pottery found with it to between about 50 BC and AD 50. It could carry a crew of several men and a heavy catch, the kind of boat Luke's scene assumes. It is now displayed at the Yigal Allon Center at Ginosar. The fisherman and historian Mendel Nun reconstructed the lake's ancient methods, including night fishing with trammel nets that the fish could not see in the dark.

The Pharisees appear here for the first time in Luke. Josephus describes them as the most accurate interpreters of the laws, holding to traditions of the fathers not written in the law of Moses, and as highly influential with ordinary people (Antiquities 13.297-298, 18.12-15); he counts about six thousand in Herod the Great's day (Antiquities 17.42). Teachers of the law, or scribes, were experts in interpreting and applying Scripture; many belonged to the Pharisaic party. Levi collected tolls at a booth, probably at Capernaum on the road near the border between the territories of Antipas and Philip. Mark 2:14 calls him Levi son of Alphaeus, while Matthew 9:9 names the same tax collector Matthew; Luke lists Matthew among the Twelve (6:15) without identifying him with Levi, and the second-century teacher Heracleon, quoted by Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 4.9), listed Matthew and Levi as two different men.
cultural:
What the Bible calls leprosy (Hebrew tsaraʿat, Greek lepra) was not only what is now called Hansen's disease, the infection whose bacillus Gerhard Armauer Hansen identified in 1873. Leviticus 13 uses the term for a range of visible skin conditions and even for mold on garments and houses (13:47-59, 14:33-53). Hansen's disease did exist in the region by Jesus' day: DNA of the leprosy bacterium was identified in a first-century burial in the Tomb of the Shroud at Akeldama in Jerusalem, published in 2009. The Law declared the sufferer ritually unclean: he was to wear torn clothes, leave his hair loose, cover his upper lip, cry out ‘Unclean’, and live apart, “He must live alone in a place outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:46). Josephus says such people could not live in a city or village (Against Apion 1.281), and the Temple Scroll from Qumran (11Q19 46:16-18) provides separate places east of the holy city for lepers and others with discharges. Rabbinic tradition treated a leper as like one dead (b. Nedarim 64b, from Numbers 12:12), and the Mishnah devotes a whole tractate, Negaim, to diagnosing these conditions. Touching such a man would ordinarily have made Jesus unclean. Instead the cleansing flows the other way. Jesus then sends the man to the priest with the offerings of Leviticus 14, a two-stage rite with birds, cedarwood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop, and on the eighth day lambs, grain, and oil, so that his restoration could be officially confirmed and he could return to worship and to his village.

Most Galilean village houses had flat roofs of wooden beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. Mark 2:4 says the men dug through the roof; Luke speaks of tiles (keramoi), the kind of roof his readers elsewhere in the Roman world would picture. Meals were more than food. To recline at table with someone was to accept him, and Pharisaic concern for purity and for tithing made table company a serious matter, since food in a careless household might not have been tithed or kept clean. Tax collectors were despised as extortioners and as collaborators handling Gentile money; the Mishnah treats a house entered by tax collectors as unclean (m. Tohorot 7:6) and permits a false vow to escape murderers, robbers, and tax collectors (m. Nedarim 3:4). Levi's banquet (dochē) is a formal reception, with guests reclining on couches in the Greco-Roman manner that Jews also used at festive meals.

The Law commanded only one fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29-31). After the exile, fasts marked the fall of Jerusalem (Zechariah 8:19), and devout people fasted more often: the Pharisee in 18:12 fasts twice a week, and the Didache (8:1), an early Christian manual of about AD 100, tells believers not to fast on Mondays and Thursdays with the ‘hypocrites’ but on Wednesdays and Fridays. Weddings lasted days, and the bridegroom's friends were exempt from religious duties that would interrupt the celebration. Wineskins were whole goat or sheep hides; new wine, still fermenting, would stretch and split an old skin that had already been stretched and dried. Ancient taste generally preferred aged wine, as Sirach 9:10 assumes.
literary:
Luke assembles five scenes that belong together. The first, the call of the fishermen (1-11), is fuller than Mark 1:16-20 and Matthew 4:18-22, which record only the call by the shore. Luke's version combines a teaching scene, a miracle, a confession, and a commission, the pattern of prophetic call stories: an encounter with God's holiness, a confession of unworthiness, a word of reassurance, and a sending, as in Isaiah 6:1-8, where the prophet cries “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). Its miraculous catch resembles the scene after the resurrection in John 21:1-14, a relationship discussed below. The address changes from ‘Master’ (verse 5) to ‘Lord’ (verse 8) as Simon's understanding grows, and Luke names him Simon Peter for the first time at the moment of confession.

The following four scenes, the leper, the paralytic, Levi, and the fasting question, follow the order of Mark 1:40-2:22. The last three are controversy stories, a form in which an action of Jesus draws criticism and his answer ends in a memorable saying. Joanna Dewey (Markan Public Debate, 1980) showed that Mark arranged the five controversies of Mark 2:1-3:6 in a concentric pattern, with the healing stories at the ends and the saying about the bridegroom's removal at the center; Luke keeps the sequence (5:17-6:11), and with it the rising tension. The paralytic scene contains one of the clearest signs that the Synoptic Gospels are literarily related: all three break off Jesus' sentence in the same place, ‘so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins’, with the same narrative aside, ‘He said to the paralytic’ (Mark 2:10, Matthew 9:6, Luke 5:24). The grumbling of the Pharisees in verse 30 uses the verb of Israel's murmuring in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7-8), a theme that returns in 15:2 and 19:7.

Luke's parable of the garment differs from Mark's: in Mark an unshrunk patch tears an old garment, while in Luke someone cuts up a new garment to patch an old one and ruins both. Luke adds verse 39, found in no other Gospel, a wry comment that people who like the old wine do not want to try the new. The chapter moves from repeated ‘leaving everything’ (verses 11 and 28) to feasting (29), and from Jesus' touch of an unclean man (13) to his table with unclean company (29-30). William Wrede (The Messianic Secret, 1901) made the commands to silence, such as verse 14, the center of a famous thesis about Mark; Luke keeps this one but lets the news spread (verse 15) and adds that Jesus withdrew to pray (verse 16), one of many notes on his prayer that are unique to Luke.

outline.t: The great catch and the call of the first disciples
Jesus touches and cleanses a leper
The paralyzed man forgiven and healed
Levi's call and banquet with tax collectors and sinners
The question about fasting: bridegroom, garments, and wineskins

doctrines.note: Simon's response to the catch is not gratitude for fish but fear before holiness: “Go away from me, Lord”, he says, “for I am a sinful man.” Like Isaiah in the temple, he sees his sin when God's power comes near. Then Jesus touches the unclean man and holiness overcomes uncleanness instead of being defiled by it, reversing what the purity laws assumed.

The scribes reason rightly that only God can forgive sins (verse 21). Jesus does not deny the premise; he claims authority on earth to forgive, proves it by healing, and calls himself the bridegroom, a role the prophets gave to God. Luke shows God's prerogatives exercised in a human life without yet explaining how.

Jesus pronounces forgiveness before he heals and sends the cleansed leper to the priest with the offering Moses prescribed. The chapter joins forgiveness, cleansing, and sacrifice, and hints in verse 35 that the bridegroom will be taken away. How Jesus can forgive so freely becomes clear at the cross, where he prays for his executioners and promises paradise to a criminal.

Jesus sees the faith of the friends who carried the paralyzed man and dug through a roof, a faith visible in action. Simon obeys a command that his experience says is pointless (because You say so, verse 5), and the leper trusts Jesus' power while asking for his will. Faith in Luke is persistent, practical, and directed to Jesus himself.

Jesus says he came to call sinners to repentance (verse 32), and Luke alone includes the final words. The call is not approval of sin but an invitation out of it, extended over a meal. Levi's leaving everything and throwing a banquet shows repentance as a new direction that becomes a welcome for others.

words.note: Epistatēs, master, overseer, one in charge. It occurs seven times in the New Testament, all in Luke and always addressed to Jesus by disciples or people seeking help (5:5, 8:24, 8:45, 9:33, 9:49, 17:13). Luke seems to use it where Mark has ‘Teacher’ or ‘Rabbi’ for Gentile readers who would not know the Hebrew title. In verse 5 it is Simon's respectful address before the miracle; in verse 8 he says ‘Lord’, kurios, a change that marks the difference the catch has made.

Hamartōlos, sinful, a sinner. It occurs about forty-seven times in the New Testament, some eighteen of them in Luke, more than any other book. It can describe anyone who sins, but in Jesus' day it also labeled people seen as living outside the Law, such as tax collectors or those in disreputable trades. In this chapter Simon applies it to himself (verse 8), and the Pharisees apply it to others (verse 30); Jesus says he came to call such people (verse 32). Luke returns to the contrast in 7:36-50, 15:1-2, 18:9-14, and 19:7.

Zōgreō, to catch alive, from zōos, alive, and agreō, to catch. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, here and in 2 Timothy 2:26, where people are held captive by the devil. In the Septuagint it describes sparing captives alive in war (Numbers 31:15, 18; Joshua 6:25). Where Mark 1:17 has ‘fishers of men’, Luke's verb says Simon will take people alive, catching for life and rescue rather than for death, a contrast with Jeremiah 16:16, where God sends fishermen to catch Israel for judgment.

Katharizō, to cleanse, make clean. It occurs about thirty-one times in the New Testament, seven in Luke (4:27, 5:12, 5:13, 7:22, 11:39, 17:14, 17:17). In the Septuagint it describes the priest's declaration that a person is clean (Leviticus 13-14) as well as actual purification. The leper asks to be made clean, not merely cured, because cleanness meant restoration to worship and community. Jesus answers with the same verb, ‘Be clean’, and the related noun katharismos, cleansing, names the offering Moses prescribed (verse 14).

Aphiēmi, to release, let go, leave, forgive. It occurs about 140 times in the New Testament with a wide range: Simon and Levi leave everything (verses 11 and 28 use related verbs), debts are released, and sins are forgiven. In verses 20 to 24 the perfect passive apheōntai, ‘your sins have been forgiven and stand forgiven’, leaves the forgiver unnamed, the question the scribes raise at once. BDAG lists forgiveness as a distinct sense, the cancellation of a debt or guilt; the verb is related to the noun aphesis, release, of 4:18.

Numphios, bridegroom. It occurs about fifteen times in the New Testament, always of a bridegroom at a wedding and, in the Gospels, often of Jesus himself (Matthew 25:1-10, Mark 2:19-20, John 3:29). The prophets describe God as Israel's husband and bridegroom (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:19-20). By calling himself the bridegroom and his disciples the wedding guests (literally ‘sons of the bridal chamber’, huioi tou numphōnos), Jesus makes his presence the reason for joy and takes a role Scripture reserves for God.

Chrēstos, good, kind, pleasant, and of food or drink, good to taste. It occurs seven times in the New Testament. In verse 39 the earliest manuscripts read ‘the old is good’ (chrēstos), where later ones read the comparative ‘better’ (chrēstoteros), which the BSB and King James Version translate. In 6:35 the same adjective describes God, who is kind to the ungrateful and wicked. The wordplay is quiet but real: the kindness of God is the new wine that satisfied drinkers of the old do not want to taste.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus doing what belongs to God. His word fills the nets where a night of professional skill had failed, and Simon's response, falling at his knees and calling him Lord, is the response Isaiah made before the holy God. Jesus answers as heavenly messengers do in Luke, “Do not be afraid” (compare 1:13, 1:30, 2:10), and turns a frightened sinner into a fisher of people. He touches the unclean without becoming unclean, and his touch accomplishes what the priest could only certify. The Talmud preserves a striking rabbinic tradition in which the Messiah is pictured sitting among the lepers at the gate of Rome, binding their wounds one at a time (b. Sanhedrin 98a), and another in which one of the Messiah's names is ‘the leper’, drawn from Isaiah 53:4, where the servant is considered stricken (b. Sanhedrin 98b). The traditions are later than the Gospels and independent of them, but they show that Jewish readers too could picture the Messiah among the untouchable.

Jesus forgives sins, and when the scribes object that only God can do so, he proves his authority by healing. He calls himself the Son of Man for the first time in Luke, a phrase that can mean simply a human being but here echoes Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man receives authority, glory, and a kingdom from the Ancient of Days. The authority Daniel saw given in heaven is now exercised on earth. Nathan had declared to David, “The LORD has taken away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13), speaking as God's messenger; Jesus speaks in his own name and backs his word with a deed only God could do.

He eats with tax collectors and sinners and describes himself as a physician who comes to the sick, the mission he will summarize after meeting Zacchaeus: to seek and to save the lost (19:10). He calls himself the bridegroom, a role the Old Testament gives to God in his love for Israel (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:19-20), and says the wedding guests cannot fast while he is with them. His hint that the bridegroom will be taken away, with a verb used only in this saying, is the first quiet shadow of his death in Luke. The new wine that bursts old skins is the joy of the kingdom arriving in his person, and Luke's final saying acknowledges, without bitterness, that people content with the old are slow to taste it.
interpretation:
The call of Simon has been read from the fathers on as a picture of the church's mission. Ambrose of Milan (Exposition of the Gospel of Luke, book 4) read Peter's boat as the church, troubled by storms in Matthew's account but filled with fish in Luke's, and the Latin of verse 4, Duc in altum, ‘put out into the deep’, became a watchword. Pope John Paul II opened his apostolic letter Novo Millennio Ineunte (6 January 2001), at the close of the Great Jubilee, with these words as a summons to the church. Augustine and Gregory the Great compared the torn nets of Luke 5 with the unbroken net of John 21, reading the first as the church in this age, mixed and strained, and the second as the church at the end, whole and perfected. Raphael's cartoon The Miraculous Draught of Fishes (1515 to 1516), designed for the tapestries that Pope Leo X commissioned for the Sistine Chapel and now in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, shows Simon kneeling before Christ in an overloaded boat.

The cleansing of the leper shaped Christian care for the sick. Francis of Assisi, in his Testament (1226), dated his conversion to the day when God led him among lepers and he showed them mercy, and what had seemed bitter became sweet. Father Damien de Veuster, who served the leprosy settlement on Molokai in Hawaii and died of the disease in 1889, became a modern emblem of the same obedience. The healing of the paralytic has been cited in the Christian debate over absolution, Catholic and Orthodox writers seeing in verse 24 the ground of the authority to forgive that Christ gave his church (John 20:23), Protestant writers stressing that the authority belongs to the Son of Man himself and is exercised through the proclaimed word.

Levi's banquet had a notable afterlife in art. Paolo Veronese painted an enormous Last Supper in 1573 for the refectory of the Dominican friary of Santi Giovanni e Paolo in Venice, crowded with soldiers, jesters, and dogs. Summoned before the Inquisition to explain the indecorum, he changed the title to The Feast in the House of Levi, citing Luke 5; the painting is now in the Gallerie dell'Accademia. Caravaggio's The Calling of Saint Matthew (1599 to 1600), in the Contarelli Chapel of San Luigi dei Francesi in Rome, paints the parallel call from Matthew 9:9 as a shaft of light falling on a tax collector's counting table.

The sayings on new wine and old wineskins became a battleground in the second century. Marcion used them to argue that Jesus' gospel had nothing to do with Israel's Law and its God, and Tertullian (Against Marcion 4.11) answered that the Creator himself had promised new things and that the distinction of new and old implies one God who gives both. Verse 39, which seemed to praise the old, is missing from Codex Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts. Modern criticism has asked how far the controversy stories reflect the early church's own debates. Rudolf Bultmann (The History of the Synoptic Tradition, 1921) argued that the forgiveness dialogue in the paralytic story was inserted to ground the church's right to forgive sins, while Geza Vermes (Jesus the Jew, 1973) argued that the Aramaic ‘son of man’ could be an ordinary way of saying ‘I’. Daniel Boyarin (The Jewish Gospels, 2012), a Jewish scholar, read Mark 2:10 as a claim that Jesus is Daniel's divine Son of Man, the kind of claim first-century Jews could understand even when they denied it of Jesus. In the Revised Common Lectionary Luke 5:1-11 is read on the fifth Sunday after the Epiphany in Year C.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts. In verse 39 the earliest manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, read ‘the old is good’ (chrēstos); later manuscripts and the Byzantine text read ‘the old is better’ (chrēstoteros), which the King James Version and the BSB translate. The positive is the harder and probably original reading: the drinker is so content with the old that he does not even compare. Codex Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts omit verse 39 entirely, perhaps because it seemed to commend the old against Jesus' new wine. In verse 38 the Byzantine text and the King James Version add ‘and both are preserved’, borrowed from Matthew 9:17.

In verses 5 and 6 the earlier manuscripts have the plural ‘nets’, where the Byzantine text and the King James Version have the singular ‘net’. In verse 17 the Byzantine text reads ‘the power of the Lord was present to heal them’, while the earliest manuscripts read ‘for Him to heal’, attributing the healing power to God's presence with Jesus. In verse 32 ‘to repentance’ belongs to Luke in all manuscripts, and later manuscripts of Matthew 9:13 and Mark 2:17 add it from Luke. In verse 20 the BSB renders the address anthrōpe, literally ‘Man’, as ‘Friend’, where Mark 2:5 has ‘Son’ (literally ‘child’).

teach.big: Jesus exercises God's own authority to call, cleanse, forgive, and welcome sinners, and the joy of his presence cannot be contained in old forms, though those content with the old are slow to receive it.

outline.t: Jesus' word overrules a professional's experience, and the nearness of his holiness leads Simon to confession, reassurance, and a new calling to catch people alive.
Jesus is both able and willing: his touch cleanses the untouchable, the Law's process restores the man to community, and the rising fame drives Jesus to prayer.
The friends' faith brings the paralytic to Jesus, who addresses the deepest need first and proves by a visible healing his invisible authority to forgive sins.
Jesus calls a despised tax collector, eats with his friends, and explains that he came as a physician to the sick, calling sinners to repentance.
The presence of the bridegroom means celebration now and fasting later, and the new life of the kingdom needs new forms, though many prefer the old.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common. The first turns the miraculous catch into a promise of business success for those who obey Jesus. The catch is a sign that points to a calling, and the fishermen respond by leaving the boats full of fish on the shore. The second treats the leper's healing as a story about disease alone and misses the social and religious exclusion that cleansing ended; Jesus restores a man to worship and community, not only to health. A third makes Jesus the enemy of the Law in the leper scene, when he sends the man to the priest with the offering Moses commanded.

With the paralytic, avoid implying that his illness was caused by his sin; the text does not say so, and John 9:1-3 warns against the assumption. With Levi's banquet, avoid preaching that Jesus simply accepted everyone as they were: he came to call sinners to repentance, and the banquet is the fruit of a man who left everything. Avoid, too, making the Pharisees cartoon villains; their concern for holiness was serious, and many Christians share their instinct to keep distance from the compromised. The new wine sayings are often used to justify every new method in church life or to dismiss tradition; their subject is the newness of the kingdom arriving in Jesus, not the relative merits of worship styles.
teach.pastoral: The leper's question, whether Jesus is willing, is the question of many who believe God can help others but doubt he wants to help them, including those living with chronic illness, disability, or shame that keeps them apart. Jesus' answer, the touch before the word, speaks to them. The paralytic's friends offer a picture of the church carrying those who cannot come on their own. Teach Simon's cry, ‘Go away from me, for I am a sinful man’, with care for the scrupulous: Jesus does not leave him in fear but says ‘Do not be afraid’ and gives him work. Those who feel unwelcome in churches because of their past or their work should hear that Jesus' first recorded meal in Luke's account of his ministry was in a tax collector's house.

hard.q: Does Jesus claim to be God when he forgives the paralytic's sins, or is he announcing God's forgiveness as a prophet or priest might?
hard.a:
The objection has Jewish, critical, and historical forms. Jewish readers note that Israel's prophets and priests could declare God's forgiveness without claiming divinity: Nathan tells David, “The LORD has taken away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13), and the priest who offered the sin offering made atonement so that the offerer was forgiven (Leviticus 4:20-35). Jesus' words in verse 20 are in the passive, ‘your sins are forgiven’, the form Jewish speech used to refer to God's action without naming him, and a fragment from Qumran, the Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242), may speak of a Jewish diviner forgiving a king's sin, though the reading is disputed. On this view the scribes' charge of blasphemy reflects later Christian claims, not Jesus' intention. Rudolf Bultmann (1921) went further and argued that verses 5b to 10 in Mark were inserted into a simple healing story to ground the church's own authority to forgive, and Geza Vermes (Jesus the Jew, 1973) argued that the Aramaic ‘son of man’ could be a modest way of saying ‘I’, not a title.

Others answer from the scene's own logic. Jesus does not say that God has forgiven, as Nathan did, or send the man to the temple, as he sent the leper to the priest; he claims that ‘the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins’, and he treats the healing as proof of a personal authority that the scribes rightly reserve to God. Darrell Bock (Blasphemy and Exaltation in Judaism, 1998) argued that the charge of blasphemy fits first-century Jewish concern for God's unique prerogatives, and Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the God of Israel, 2008) that the Gospels include Jesus within the unique identity of Israel's God by giving him God's own acts, forgiving sins among them. Daniel Boyarin (The Jewish Gospels, 2012), writing as a Jewish scholar, reads the passage as a claim that Jesus is Daniel's divine Son of Man, a category he thinks some first-century Jews already held, while denying that Jesus was that figure. The church confesses that Jesus forgives as only God can. The historical questions about how the saying was shaped remain debated, and the Jewish objection, that no man may take God's place, is the objection the scribes themselves raise in verse 21.

hard.q: How does Luke's call of Simon relate to Mark 1:16-20 and to the catch of fish in John 21?
hard.a:
The problem is plain. In Mark 1:16-20 and Matthew 4:18-22 Jesus walks by the lake and calls Simon, Andrew, James, and John from their nets, and they follow at once; there is no miracle and no confession, and the call comes before any healing at Capernaum. Luke puts the call after Jesus has healed Simon's mother-in-law, omits Andrew, and adds a miraculous catch. John 21:1-14 tells of a night of fruitless fishing, a command to let down the net, an enormous catch, and a scene centered on Simon Peter, but sets it after the resurrection. Many critical scholars, Raymond Brown among them (The Gospel according to John, Anchor Bible, 1970), have concluded that Luke and John preserve one tradition, originally a resurrection appearance to Peter, which Luke moved into the ministry and joined to Mark's call story; Peter's confession of sinfulness would then fit a man who had denied his Lord.

Other scholars, among them Darrell Bock (Luke 1:1-9:50, 1994), hold that the two catches are different events and that the second deliberately recalls the first: in Luke the nets begin to tear and Peter asks Jesus to leave, while in John the net holds and Peter leaps into the water to reach him, and the risen Jesus restores the disciple by repeating the scene of his first calling. The difference from Mark can also be read as complementary. John 1:35-42 records an earlier meeting between Jesus and Andrew and Simon near the Jordan, and Luke's own order shows Simon hearing Jesus teach and seeing his mother-in-law healed before he leaves his nets, which would explain the readiness Mark reports without explanation. Scholars who hold a high view of Scripture differ on these questions, and nothing in the church's confession depends on the answer. What the three accounts share is Peter's calling by grace, through a word of Jesus, to a work he could not have chosen for himself.

observe: What does Simon call Jesus in verse 5, and what does he call him in verse 8? What happened in between?
What does Jesus do for the man with leprosy before he speaks, and where does he send him afterward?
Who complains about Jesus in verses 21, 30, and 33, and what exactly does each complaint object to?
interpret: Why does the great catch make Simon aware of his sin rather than simply grateful?
Why does Jesus forgive the paralyzed man before healing him, and how does the healing answer the scribes' objection?
What do the images of the bridegroom, the garment, and the wineskins say about what is new in Jesus' coming, and what does verse 39 add?
apply: The leper was sure Jesus could heal but unsure he was willing. Where do you doubt not God's power but his willingness toward you?
The paralyzed man reached Jesus because his friends carried him and broke through a roof. Who has carried you, and whom might you carry?
Jesus ate with people the respectable avoided. Whose table would he sit at in your town, and would you be comfortable there with him?
